description: The twelve factors that shape self-concept and six evidence-based strategies for building resilience.
hero_image_caption: A support worker and young person in conversation at a community centre.
content_html:
What Shapes Self-Concept?

Self-concept — how an individual thinks about, evaluates and perceives themselves — is not fixed at birth. It is constantly shaped and reshaped by a wide range of factors throughout life. Some of these factors have a positive influence, strengthening an individual’s sense of worth and identity. Others have a negative influence, undermining self-esteem and making it harder for someone to see their own value. The specification identifies twelve factors that affect self-concept, and understanding how each one works — and how they interact — is central to this topic.

The Twelve Factors

The twelve factors can be grouped to make them easier to remember. The first group relates to personal characteristics and experiences: age, appearance, gender and sexuality. The second group relates to social and relational influences: relationships with others, culture and education. The third group relates to adversity and discrimination: abuse, stereotyping and discrimination, unconscious bias and social media. The twelfth factor — life experiences — acts as an overarching category that can encompass many of the others.

Key Fact

The twelve factors affecting self-concept are: abuse, age, appearance, culture, education, emotional development, gender, income, life experiences, relationships with others, sexuality, social media, stereotyping and discrimination, and unconscious bias. (Note: some versions of the spec list 12 distinct factors; always learn from the most recent published version and your notes.)

Positive and Negative Influences

Each factor can operate as a positive or negative influence depending on the individual’s circumstances. Stereotyping and discrimination almost always harm self-concept — when a person is repeatedly told, either explicitly or through others’ behaviour, that they are “less than”, they begin to internalise that message. Research consistently links experiences of racism, sexism or homophobia to lower self-esteem and poorer mental health outcomes.

By contrast, positive relationships with others are among the most powerful constructive forces on self-concept. When a parent consistently encourages a child, when a teacher notices and names a student’s strengths, or when a care worker treats a service user with genuine respect, the individual’s sense of their own worth is reinforced. Consider 14-year-old Daniil, who has just moved schools. His new form tutor regularly praises his contributions in class and pairs him with a supportive peer mentor. Within a few weeks, Daniil’s self-confidence has improved noticeably. Positive relationships at a critical life stage can offset the negative effects of other factors.

Age affects self-concept in different ways at different life stages. Adolescents are particularly vulnerable to self-concept fluctuations as they negotiate their identity. Older adults in later adulthood may face ageist assumptions about their capabilities — being spoken to slowly, being left out of decisions — which can damage their sense of self-worth.

Appearance is significant because society attaches value to physical looks, particularly in adolescence. A young person whose appearance does not match cultural ideals of attractiveness may experience lower self-esteem. Positive feedback about appearance from trusted people can counteract this.

Social media is a contemporary factor with significant negative potential. Constant comparison to curated, filtered images of others can lead individuals to feel their own lives or bodies are inadequate. For young people in particular, the social validation of likes and followers can become a measure of self-worth — making self-concept unstable and dependent on external approval.

Unconscious bias occurs when practitioners or peers make automatic assumptions about individuals based on characteristics such as race, gender or disability — without realising they are doing so. For the service user, repeated experiences of unconscious bias can lead to internalised negative self-concept: they begin to believe they are less capable or less valued than others.

How Factors Interrelate

The twelve factors do not operate in isolation. Income, for instance, affects the environment a person grows up in, the education they can access, their appearance (including the clothes and products available to them), and the relationships they are able to maintain. A child growing up in poverty may face multiple simultaneous negative influences on their self-concept. Conversely, strong emotional development — developed through secure early attachments — can buffer an individual against the harmful effects of other factors. Mark schemes on this topic often reward candidates who can identify two factors and explain how each affects self-concept, with examples.

Key Fact

Factors affecting self-concept can be positive (supportive relationships, educational achievement, positive life experiences) or negative (abuse, discrimination, social media comparison, unconscious bias). The same factor can work in either direction depending on the individual’s circumstances.

Six Strategies for Developing Resilience

Resilience — the ability to adapt successfully to life’s unexpected challenges — can be developed. The specification identifies six named strategies that support resilience-building. Practitioners in care settings use these strategies to help service users manage adversity more effectively.

1. Self-reflection and learning from past difficulties. Individuals who take time to reflect on how they have managed previous challenges begin to recognise patterns in their own resilience. A social worker might encourage a care leaver to think about a difficult transition they have already navigated and identify what helped them at the time.

2. Recognising personal strengths and qualities. Many individuals who have experienced adversity struggle to identify their own strengths. Practitioners support resilience by helping individuals name their capabilities — “you managed that difficult conversation really well; that took courage.” Recognising strengths provides a foundation for self-concept and for facing future challenges.

3. Positive interactions with others. Maintaining supportive relationships — with friends, family, peers or practitioners — provides the emotional scaffolding that helps individuals manage difficult times. Feeling heard and valued by others reinforces a positive self-concept, which in turn supports resilience.

4. Participating in new activities. Taking on new experiences — joining a sports club, starting a course, volunteering — builds competence and confidence. Each successful new experience adds to an individual’s evidence that they are capable, which strengthens both self-concept and the capacity to adapt.

5. Achievements, praise and rewards. External recognition matters, particularly during periods of low self-esteem. When a care worker acknowledges that a service user has reached a goal — however small — it reinforces positive self-concept and motivates continued effort. This is not about empty praise, but about honest recognition of genuine progress.

6. Understanding personal limits and setting realistic goals. Resilience is not about pushing through regardless of cost. Individuals who understand their own boundaries — who can say “I need a break” or “that is too much for me right now” — are less likely to experience burnout or crisis. Setting realistic, achievable goals means progress is possible and self-concept is maintained, rather than being repeatedly undermined by unachievable targets.
exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark question asking you to identify two factors affecting self-concept and explain how each works, the most common error is giving two factors that are so similar they cannot be awarded two separate marks — for example, “discrimination” and “stereotyping”, which are listed as one combined factor. Make sure your two chosen factors are genuinely distinct items from the list of twelve. Then for each factor, use the word “because” to show how it affects self-concept, not just that it does. For example: “Social media negatively affects self-concept because young people compare themselves to filtered images of others, leading them to feel inadequate, therefore lowering their self-esteem.”
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Twelve factors shape self-concept — including age, appearance, relationships, culture, income, abuse, social media, stereotyping and discrimination, and unconscious bias — and each can work positively or negatively depending on circumstances.
  • The six resilience strategies are: self-reflection on past difficulties, recognising personal strengths, positive interactions with others, participating in new activities, achievements and praise, and setting realistic goals.
  • Factors do not operate in isolation — income, education, relationships and emotional development interact, and high-tariff exam answers show how multiple factors compound each other.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is one of the twelve factors that can affect self-concept?
A) Resilience
B) Active participation
C) Unconscious bias
D) Well-being
practice_questions.marks: C) Unconscious bias [1 mark]. Resilience, active participation and well-being are related concepts but are not listed among the twelve factors affecting self-concept.

practice_questions.text: Give two ways in which social media can negatively affect an individual's self-concept.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct, accurate points (max 2). Acceptable answers: constant comparison to filtered/curated images leads to feelings of inadequacy [1]; relying on likes and followers as a measure of self-worth makes self-concept unstable and dependent on external approval [1]; cyberbullying via social media platforms damages self-esteem [1]. Two near-identical points score 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: Explain how stereotyping and discrimination can negatively affect a person's self-concept.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying the effect (experiencing stereotyping or discrimination leads to lower self-esteem / negative self-concept); 1 mark for a developed reason using 'because' (e.g. because repeated messages that a person is inferior or 'less than' are internalised over time); 1 mark for a further development or example (e.g. therefore the individual begins to believe these negative messages about themselves, which affects their emotional well-being and their willingness to engage with education, employment or social opportunities).

practice_questions.text: Describe two strategies a key worker at a residential care home could use to help an older adult develop resilience following a bereavement.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per strategy, applied to the care home context. Example: Recognising personal strengths and qualities (2 marks) — 1 mark for naming the strategy; 1 mark for describing a specific key-worker action with reference to the care home setting (e.g. the key worker meets regularly with the resident to discuss a skill or quality they have demonstrated that week, such as showing patience during a physiotherapy session, so that the resident begins to recognise their own capabilities). Setting realistic goals (2 marks) — 1 mark for naming the strategy; 1 mark for a specific example (e.g. agreeing with the resident that they will attend one group activity per week rather than expecting full re-engagement with social life immediately). Other strategies accepted with equivalent development.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how two factors affecting self-concept can interact to produce a compounded negative effect on an individual's well-being.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Selects two distinct factors from the twelve and explains each separately, then shows how they interact to produce a compounded effect. Uses 'because', 'therefore', 'this means that'. Example content: Income affects self-concept negatively because poverty restricts the individual's access to resources associated with social acceptance (clothing, activities, food) [1], therefore the individual may feel different from peers and develop low self-esteem [1]. Education interacts with income: a person from a low-income background may attend a school with fewer resources, limiting their academic achievement [1], which reduces their sense of capability and reinforces a negative self-concept [1]. Together, low income and limited educational achievement create a compounding effect — each factor makes the negative impact of the other worse, reducing the individual's overall sense of worth and future prospects [2].

Secure (3–4 marks): Addresses both factors with some development; the interaction is identified but not fully explored.

Developing (2 marks): Describes both factors in isolation without showing how they interact.

Emerging (1 mark): Names one factor with minimal explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Kolade is 17 years old and has recently left care. He struggled at school, has a difficult relationship with his family, and has low self-esteem. He is now living independently in a supported housing placement. His support worker wants to help him develop a more positive self-concept and build resilience.

Evaluate how effectively the six resilience strategies could support Kolade's well-being in his current situation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9–10 marks): Selects at least four of the six strategies, evaluates each with specific reference to Kolade's circumstances (care leaver, low self-esteem, difficult family relationships, independent living), and makes a balanced overall judgement about effectiveness. Example content: Self-reflection — supports Kolade because care leavers have often managed significant adversity; reflecting on past difficulties he has overcome provides evidence of his own resilience [positive]; however, if reflection focuses primarily on failure (school struggles, family breakdown) without skilled facilitation by the support worker, it could reinforce negative self-concept [limitation]. Recognising personal strengths — highly relevant given Kolade's low self-esteem; the support worker's role is to identify and name strengths he cannot yet see himself [positive]. Participating in new activities — supported housing often provides opportunities for this; each successful new experience adds to Kolade's evidence of capability [positive]; however, anxiety or past rejection may make trying new things threatening [limitation]. Setting realistic goals — essential for Kolade, who may have experienced only unachievable targets in school; small, achievable milestones (e.g. attending college interview) protect self-concept [positive]. Conclusion: all six strategies have potential, but their effectiveness depends on the quality of the support worker relationship and Kolade's readiness to engage. The strategies work best in combination, not isolation.

Secure (6–8 marks): Addresses most strategies with relevant reference to Kolade; some evaluation of effectiveness.

Developing (3–5 marks): Describes some strategies with limited evaluation; application to Kolade is partial.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Names one or two strategies with minimal application.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the twelve factors affecting self-concept?
Which resilience strategy involves taking time to think about how you have coped with difficulties in the past?
options: Self-reflection and learning from past difficulties

knowledge_checks.q: Assumptions that operate below conscious awareness and influence judgements without the person realising are called _____ bias.
The resilience strategy of understanding personal _____ helps individuals avoid burnout by recognising when they need to stop or seek support.
Match each resilience strategy to its description:
right: Naming your own capabilities to build a foundation for facing future challenges
Maintaining supportive relationships that provide emotional scaffolding
Choosing achievable targets so progress is possible and self-concept is maintained

flashcard_questions.q: How many factors affecting self-concept does the specification list?
Give three factors that affect self-concept involving personal characteristics.
How does stereotyping and discrimination typically affect self-concept?
flashcard_questions.a: Individuals internalise negative messages about themselves, leading to lower self-esteem.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is social media identified as a factor that negatively affects self-concept?
flashcard_questions.a: Comparison to filtered images and reliance on likes makes self-concept unstable.
Assumptions that operate below conscious awareness, influencing behaviour without the person realising.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the six resilience strategies from the specification.
flashcard_questions.a: Self-reflection, recognising strengths, positive interactions, new activities, achievements/praise, realistic goals.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the resilience strategy 'participating in new activities' build?
flashcard_questions.a: Competence and confidence through successful new experiences.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is praise and recognition important for building resilience?
flashcard_questions.a: It reinforces positive self-concept and motivates continued effort during low self-esteem.

flashcard_questions.q: How does setting realistic goals protect self-concept?
flashcard_questions.a: Achievable targets mean progress is possible, preventing repeated experience of failure.

flashcard_questions.q: How can income negatively affect self-concept?
flashcard_questions.a: Poverty restricts access to resources associated with social acceptance, causing feelings of inadequacy.

flashcard_questions.q: Why can positive relationships with others support resilience?
flashcard_questions.a: Feeling heard and valued by others reinforces positive self-concept, which helps individuals manage adversity.

flashcard_questions.q: Can the same factor affect self-concept both positively and negatively?
flashcard_questions.a: Yes — it depends on the individual's specific circumstances.

glossary_terms.definition: Significant events and experiences that have occurred during an individual's life, which shape how they see themselves and interact with the world.
The way an individual or group are treated as inferior or different based on a characteristic such as age, gender, race or sexuality, regardless of their actual behaviour or abilities.
Assumptions or preferences about individuals or groups that operate below conscious awareness, influencing behaviour and judgements without the person realising.

items.title: Grit: The Power of Passion and Perseverance | Angela Duckworth | TED
items.description: Duckworth's research on grit — the long-term effort behind success — directly maps onto the resilience strategies of setting realistic goals and learning from past difficulties.

items.title: How One Tweet Can Ruin Your Life | Jon Ronson | TED
items.description: Examines how social media shaming damages self-concept — a vivid case study for the social media factor affecting self-esteem.

items.title: Listening to Shame | Brené Brown | TED
items.description: Brown explores how shame — often triggered by stereotyping and discrimination — erodes self-concept, and how vulnerability can rebuild it.

items.title: 13th (2016)
items.description: Ava DuVernay's documentary on race and inequality in America — a powerful illustration of how systemic stereotyping and discrimination shape identity and self-concept over generations.

items.title: Young Minds — Resilience Toolkit
items.description: Young Minds' practical resource covering all six resilience strategies from a youth mental health perspective — matches the specification list directly.

items.title: Anna Freud Centre — Self-Esteem and Identity
items.description: The Anna Freud Centre's resource on identity and self-esteem in young people — useful for understanding how the twelve factors play out in adolescence.

items.title: Mind — What Affects Mental Health?
items.description: Mind's accessible summary of the social and personal factors that shape mental well-being — maps directly onto several of the twelve self-concept factors.

items.title: NHS — Raising Self-Esteem
items.description: NHS guidance on improving self-esteem, including practical strategies that align with the specification's resilience-building approaches.
